description: Soy una persona proactiva y ordenada, con experiencia en construir prototipos que funcionan. Quiero un equipo donde todos aporten desde lo que mejor saben, con buena comunicación y objetivos claros, para entregar un proyecto completo y bien presentado. No necesitas ser experto: lo importante es tener ganas de aprender y colaborar.
summary: We built the CLPS Lunar Mission Navigator, a web app for comparing landing sites and dates near the Moon’s south pole. For each site it shows the share of time with Sun, the longest night, the share of time with Earth in view (direct communication), and the longest communication gap. It also provides timelines and a horizon view with the Sun and Earth drawn to angular scale. Positions are computed with astronomy-engine and the IAU 2009 lunar orientation model, and checked against NASA’s JPL Horizons (agreement within 0.01°) and PyEphem. It gives mission planners, educators and the public a quick first look that would otherwise require specialized tools. This matters because at the south pole the Sun and Earth stay near the horizon, so power and communications trade off against each other. For now it uses an adjustable flat horizon, without real LOLA terrain.
details:
CLPS Lunar Mission Navigator is an interactive web app for comparing solar illumination and Earth visibility at potential landing sites near the lunar south pole.

Users pick a start date and an analysis period (14 days, 30 days, 90 days or one year) and compare up to six locations side by side, choosing from eight preset sites or entering their own coordinates.

For each location, the app computes the position of the Sun and Earth hour by hour and reports four indicators:

  • Sunlit: share of the time the site receives sunlight.
  • Longest night: the longest continuous period without sunlight.
  • Earth in view: share of the time Earth is above the horizon, which shows whether a direct communication link is possible.
  • Longest link gap: the longest continuous period with Earth out of view.

Each location has two separate timelines, one for sunlight and one for Earth visibility. The app also draws the local horizon with both bodies at angular scale, with a time slider and a playback mode to watch how their positions change.

What are the benefits?

The tool turns information that normally requires astronomical models and specialized software into a comparison that takes seconds. Its main benefit is making it easy to compare locations on two factors that are critical for a lunar mission: available solar power and opportunities to communicate with Earth.

For example, over one year starting January 1, 2027, Malapert has Earth in view 67.5% of the time, while Shackleton crater, right next to the pole, reaches only 46.8%. In the flat-horizon model Shackleton gets more sunlight (56.5% versus 51.0% at Malapert); in reality its floor lies in permanent shadow, which is exactly why adding real terrain is our next step.

Seeing these numbers side by side makes the trade-off between power and connectivity visible, without relying only on data tables.

What is the intended impact?

The project aims to support mission planners in the early stages of landing site evaluation, helping them quickly spot and set aside locations with less favorable conditions.

It also aims to bring lunar exploration closer to students and the general public, by showing how the Sun and Earth, sitting so close to the horizon at the south pole, can constrain both power generation and communications for future missions.

Tools and technologies

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS: a single-page web app that runs without a server.
  • astronomy-engine: library used to compute the astronomical positions of the Sun and the Moon.
  • IAU 2009 lunar orientation model: our own implementation to determine the Moon’s orientation and compute where each body appears from every site.
  • Python and PyEphem: used to validate the astronomical results. On 80 dates between 2026 and 2030, the computed direction of Earth differs by less than 0.03° and that of the Sun by less than 0.3°.
  • NASA JPL Horizons System: used to cross-check the app’s Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation at Malapert and Shackleton on 31 daily dates (November 14 to December 14, 2026). They agree within 0.01°.
  • Artificial intelligence (Claude, by Anthropic): used as an assistant during development, supporting implementation and technical problem-solving. The project’s architecture, integration and validation are the team’s work. AI was also used to produce the demo video (animations and an AI-generated narration voice, Kokoro TTS; the video carries a visible AI-generated label) and to write and translate the documentation and this description into English.

How is it creative and innovative?

The project brings astronomical computation, interactive visualization and data comparison together in a single, accessible tool. Its main innovative elements are:

  • Angular horizon view: shows the apparent size and position of the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon, making real visibility conditions easier to grasp.
  • Side-by-side comparison: shows several locations at once and automatically flags the best result for each indicator.
  • Custom locations: users can raise the local horizon and add their own coordinates, going beyond the preset sites.
  • Accessibility: technical information in an intuitive interface, designed so both specialists and people without an astronomy background can read the results.

Factors we considered

1. Audience and accessibility

We wanted an interface that both specialists and the general public can use, without giving up accuracy in the astronomical calculations.

2. Transparency and model limitations

The horizon is currently a flat surface: it does not include the Moon’s real topography or the LOLA elevation data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). The results are therefore useful for preliminary comparisons, but should not be used as the final criterion for choosing a landing site. The coordinates of the preset sites are approximate.

3. Scope of the communications analysis

The analysis only checks whether Earth is above the local horizon. It does not include further constraints such as minimum antenna elevation, the characteristics of the communications system or ground-station availability.

4. Validation

Calculations were cross-checked with PyEphem and with NASA’s JPL Horizons System: for Malapert and Shackleton, the Sun’s and Earth’s azimuth and elevation agree with Horizons within 0.01°. We did not use NASA’s SPICE toolkit directly, and these checks are our own, not an official NASA validation.

5. Future work

The next step is to add LOLA topography to replace the flat horizon with the real lunar relief. This would let us compute terrain obstructions, improve the accuracy of illumination and visibility periods, and bring the tool closer to a complete assessment model for future lunar missions.
